newsitem.title: USA: Russia says Japan dispute could last a generation.
newsitem.headline: Russia says Japan dispute could last a generation.

text.p: Russia's chief spokesman said on Sunday his country's long-standing dispute with Japan over four Pacific islands was unlikely to be resolved this generation.

Sergei Yastrzhembsky, spokesman to President Boris Yeltsin, advised Japan to invest in Russia's reforming economy to create a "new psychological atmosphere" that would allow the next generation to find a solution to the territorial problem.

Ties between Moscow and Tokyo have been strained for decades by the dispute over the islands seized by the Soviet army in the final days of World War Two, preventing the two sides from signing a formal post-war peace treaty.
Japan says the islands of Kunashiri, Etorofu, Habomai and Shikotan, which it terms the Northern Territories and which Russia calls the southern Kuriles, must be returned.
But Yeltsin, aware that territorial concessions would prompt a fierce backlash from his nationalist opponents, has resisted the demand, as his Soviet predecessors did.
"It's not a question for these days, for today," Yastrzhembsky said in a live on-line interview with Colorado University students during the Group of Seven summit in Denver.
"It may be the next generation could make some smart decision and resolve this problem," he said.
"Nowadays, no Russian leaders, neither (the) Russian population, is ready to make a decision about this question," Yastrzhembsky said, speaking in English.

The spokesman said that for this reason Moscow was advising Japan to increase its involvement in Russia's post-communist reforms and step up investments in Russia "to create the best atmosphere for the best understanding between the two nations".
"Why (do) we propose it? Because this economic cooperation, as we think, could create a new psychological atmosphere between Russia and Japan," Yastrzhembsky said.
"Cooperating, we will understand each other better and it could create new opportunities for new approaches to this so- called territorial problem," he added.
The G7 summit has seen some modest signs of detente between Russia and Japan.
Russia told Japanese leaders Friday that it would stop targeting missiles at Japan -- a symbolic gesture of little military significance -- and would set up a telephone hotline with Tokyo.
The two sides also agreed to hold regular summit meetings between Yeltsin and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, and approved a plan to boost Japanese investment in Russia.
Yastrzhembsky said Friday that the territorial dispute had not figured in the two countries' bilateral talks in Denver, which dealt with fishing rights and economic cooperation.

Partly because of the territorial dispute, Japan has been reluctant to countenance Russia's goal of full membership of the G7 -- which comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
A Japanese spokesman said Friday that Russia was "not ready" to join G7 discussions on issues like finance and macro-economic policy.
